title: Object Storage
objectives: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Object stores are durable (11 nines), cheap and scale infinitely. Clients upload directly with pre-signed URLs; metadata goes to a DB; processing runs async.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client asks for upload URL” to “CDN serves”, via “Pre-signed URL”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Storing images as BLOBs in the relational DB.

questions.prompt: Why use pre-signed URLs for uploads?

choices.label: Clients upload directly without routing bytes through app servers

questions.explanation: App servers stay free of heavy traffic.

questions.prompt: 1M uploads/day, 2 MB each. Storage added per year in TB (decimal)?
assumptions: Use rounded daily volume ÷ 86,400 unless stated otherwise.
questions.explanation: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB/day × 365 = 730 TB.

questions.prompt: Object storage durability?

choices.label: Yes. It is signed, not encrypted.
Long-lived token to get new short-lived access tokens.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: ~99.999999999% (11 nines).

flashcards.back: Metadata in DB, bytes in object store.

title: HDFS
objectives: Explain block replication and rack awareness
Know where HDFS fits and where it does not

cards.title: Big files, big blocks
cards.body: HDFS stores huge files split into large blocks (128 MB by default) across many DataNodes. One NameNode keeps the metadata: which blocks make up a file and where they live.

cards.title: Replication
cards.body: Each block is stored three times by default, with copies on different racks so a rack power failure does not lose data. Lost replicas are re-copied automatically.

cards.title: Reading a file
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client asks NameNode for block locations” to “NameNode never touches the data”, via “NameNode returns DataNodes per block”.
steps: Client asks NameNode for block locations
Client streams blocks directly from DataNodes

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using HDFS for millions of tiny files or low-latency lookups. Each file costs NameNode memory, and HDFS is built for large sequential scans, not serving user requests.

questions.prompt: Why are HDFS replicas placed on different racks?

choices.label: So a rack-level failure does not lose every copy
Because racks cannot hold more than one block

questions.explanation: Rack awareness protects against correlated failures.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a poor fit for HDFS?

choices.label: Nightly batch analytics over 10 TB of logs
Storing large Parquet files for Spark
Serving 50 million 2 KB profile images to users with low latency

questions.explanation: Tiny files overload NameNode memory and HDFS is not built for low-latency serving.

questions.prompt: Order an HDFS read.

items.label: Client asks NameNode for block locations

questions.explanation: Metadata from the NameNode, data straight from DataNodes.

flashcards.back: Metadata: file to block mapping and block locations, not the data.
Three copies, spread across racks.
Large sequential batch reads, not tiny files or low-latency lookups.

title: Inverted Index & Elasticsearch
objectives: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: An inverted index maps terms → documents. Analysers tokenise, lowercase and stem. Keep the DB as source of truth and sync to the search cluster via CDC or events.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 6 steps from “Write to DB” to “ranked results”, via “CDC event”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using SQL LIKE "%term%" on millions of rows for search.

questions.prompt: Why not use LIKE "%paneer%" for search?

choices.label: It cannot use a normal B-tree index and scans rows

questions.explanation: Leading wildcards force a full scan.

questions.prompt: Select features of a search engine.
questions.explanation: Search clusters are not transactional sources of truth.

questions.prompt: Inverted index?

choices.label: Skipping scale numbers, ignoring retries/idempotency, or mixing AuthN with AuthZ.
Connect user journeys to SLOs, then justify components and trade-offs for Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: Term → list of document IDs.

title: MapReduce & Spark
objectives: Process unbounded event streams in real time with windows and state (Flink, Kafka Streams).

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Tumbling, sliding and session windows aggregate events. Watermarks handle late events. Use for fraud detection, live dashboards and surge pricing.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Process unbounded event streams in real time with windows and state (Flink, Kafka Streams).

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Events stream in” to “Emit surge multiplier”, via “Key by geohash”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using batch jobs for decisions that must happen in seconds.

questions.prompt: Real-time card fraud scoring fits:
questions.explanation: Decisions are needed within milliseconds-seconds.

questions.prompt: Tumbling vs Sliding: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Windows turn infinite streams into finite aggregates.

questions.prompt: Tumbling window?

choices.label: Flag that disables a feature instantly.
An intercepted authorization code being redeemed by another app.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: Fixed-size, non-overlapping windows.

flashcards.back: Fixed-size, non-overlapping windows.
Estimate of event-time progress for late data.

title: Stream Processing
objectives: Explain windows and event time vs processing time

cards.title: Results while data flows
cards.body: Batch jobs answer questions about yesterday. Stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) update answers continuously, such as fraud scores within seconds of a UPI transaction.

cards.title: Windows
cards.body: Streams are unbounded, so you aggregate over windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) or session (gaps of inactivity). Use event time, when it happened, not processing time, when it arrived.

cards.title: Counting clicks per minute
cards.body: 4 steps from “Clicks land in Kafka” to “Results written to a store for dashboards”, via “Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window”.
steps: Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window
Watermark decides when a window closes
Results written to a store for dashboards

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Assuming events arrive in order and exactly once. Mobile clients send late events and brokers redeliver, so use watermarks for lateness and idempotent or transactional sinks for duplicates.

questions.prompt: Phones go offline and upload clicks 10 minutes late. Which time should per-minute click counts use?

choices.label: Processing time, so late clicks count in the minute they arrive
Event time, with a watermark that allows some lateness

questions.explanation: Event time puts each click in the minute it actually happened.

questions.prompt: Which is a good fit for stream processing rather than a nightly batch?

choices.label: Flagging a suspicious UPI transaction within seconds
Rebuilding a search index once a week

questions.explanation: Fraud decisions lose value with every second of delay.

questions.prompt: The broker redelivers some messages after a consumer restart. What keeps counts correct?

choices.label: Idempotent or transactional writes to the sink

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery needs deduplication or transactions at the sink.

flashcards.back: When the event happened vs when the system saw it.
Fixed-size, non-overlapping time buckets.
How long to wait for late events before closing a window.

title: Warehouse/Lake/OLAP
objectives: OLTP serves transactions; OLAP column stores serve aggregates over huge datasets.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Row stores suit point reads/writes. Column stores (ClickHouse, BigQuery) compress columns and scan aggregates fast. Time-series DBs handle append-heavy metrics with downsampling.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: OLTP serves transactions; OLAP column stores serve aggregates over huge datasets.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “App writes OLTP” to “Dashboards”, via “CDC / ETL”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Running heavy analytical queries on the production OLTP database.

questions.prompt: Best store for "average delivery time per city per hour over 2 years"?
questions.explanation: Column stores scan aggregates efficiently.

questions.prompt: Checkout transaction vs Yearly revenue report: which pairing is correct?

choices.label: Yearly revenue report → OLTP row store

questions.explanation: Separate workloads protect production.

questions.prompt: OLTP vs OLAP?

choices.label: Skipping scale numbers, ignoring retries/idempotency, or mixing AuthN with AuthZ.
OAuth grants delegated access; OIDC adds identity via an ID token.
Services verify them locally with a public key, no auth-server call.

questions.explanation: From the lesson: Transactions vs analytics.

flashcards.back: Transactions vs analytics.

title: Geospatial Indexing
objectives: Answer “nearby” queries without scanning every row
Handle cell boundaries and dense cities

cards.title: Nearby without a full scan
cards.body: Computing distance to every restaurant in India per request is too slow. Geospatial indexes bucket locations into cells so a query only checks nearby cells.

cards.title: Geohash and quadtrees
cards.body: Geohash encodes lat/long into a string; a shared prefix means nearby. Quadtrees split space into four until each cell holds few points, so dense Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas get big ones.

cards.title: Finding restaurants within 2 km
cards.body: 4 steps from “Get user’s geohash cell” to “Compute exact distance and sort”, via “Add the 8 neighbouring cells”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Searching only the user’s own cell. A restaurant 50 m away can sit across a cell boundary, so always include neighbouring cells.

questions.prompt: A user stands at the edge of a geohash cell. Why also search the neighbouring cells?

choices.label: Close results may sit just across the boundary

questions.explanation: Prefix matching misses close points across boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why might a quadtree beat fixed-size grid cells for India?

choices.label: It is always exact with no distance check
It adapts: small cells in dense cities, large ones in sparse areas

questions.explanation: Adaptive cells keep the number of points per cell manageable.

questions.prompt: Order a “nearby within 2 km” query.
questions.explanation: Coarse cell filter first, exact distance last.

flashcards.front: What does a shared geohash prefix mean?
flashcards.back: The points are close (with edge cases at cell boundaries).

flashcards.front: Why do quadtrees suit uneven density?
flashcards.back: They split dense areas into smaller cells.
Nearby points can fall just across a cell boundary.

cards.title: Append-heavy, time-ordered
cards.body: Metrics, sensor readings and prices arrive as timestamped points, mostly appended and read as ranges (last hour, last week). Time-series databases compress and index for exactly that.

cards.title: Retention and rollups
cards.body: Raw 10-second points for 7 days, 1-minute averages for 90 days, hourly for years. Downsampling keeps dashboards fast and storage bounded.

cards.title: A metric’s life
cards.body: 5 steps from “Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}” to “Raw data expires after retention”, via “Ingest appends to the current time block”.
steps: Ingest appends to the current time block

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Putting user IDs or request IDs in labels. Every unique label combination is a new series, so cardinality explodes and memory with it.

questions.prompt: Metrics memory jumped 50× after a deploy. The new label is user_id. Why?

choices.label: Each user creates a separate series, exploding cardinality

questions.explanation: Put high-cardinality values in logs or traces, not metric labels.

questions.prompt: Dashboards over 1 year of 10-second data are slow and storage is growing. What helps most?

choices.label: Downsample old data to coarser rollups with tiered retention
Store every point forever at full resolution

questions.explanation: Rollups shrink both storage and query work.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most time-series shaped?
questions.explanation: Timestamped, append-only, read by range.

flashcards.back: Replacing old raw points with coarser aggregates like 1-minute averages.
Unbounded label values such as user or request IDs.
A range scan over a time window for a series.

title: Blue-Green/Canary/Feature Flags
objectives: Use feature flags and kill switches safely

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.body: Run two full environments. Deploy to the idle one (green), test it, then switch the router from blue to green. Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the switch, and database changes must work for both.

cards.title: Canary
cards.body: Send a small share of traffic (1%, then 5%, 25%) to the new version and watch error rates and latency. Roll back automatically if they get worse. It catches problems only real traffic shows.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.body: Ship code dark and turn features on per user, region or percentage at runtime. Kill switches turn a broken feature off without a deploy. Remove flags once rolled out, or they pile up as untested paths.

cards.title: A canary rollout
cards.body: 5 steps from “Deploy v2 next to v1” to “Roll back if metrics worsen”, via “Route 1% of traffic to v2”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Shipping a schema change the old version cannot read, then rolling back. Make changes backward compatible: add the new column, switch code, remove the old column later.

questions.prompt: What does a canary release do?

choices.label: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate
Switches all traffic at once and rolls back if users complain
Deploys to every server at 2 AM

questions.explanation: Real traffic, limited blast radius.

questions.prompt: In blue-green, how do you roll back?

choices.label: Redeploy the old build to every server
Point the router back to the old environment

questions.explanation: The old environment is still running.

questions.prompt: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?

choices.label: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag

questions.explanation: Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

questions.prompt: Order a canary rollout.
questions.explanation: Grow only while metrics hold.

questions.prompt: Order a rollback-safe column rename.

items.label: Switch reads to the new column

questions.explanation: Every step works with the previous code version.

flashcards.front: What does a canary release do?
flashcards.back: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate. Real traffic, limited blast radius.

flashcards.front: In blue-green, how do you roll back?
flashcards.back: Point the router back to the old environment. The old environment is still running.

flashcards.front: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?
flashcards.back: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag. Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals
Use readiness vs liveness probes correctly

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: 5 steps from “New image pushed” to “One old pod is removed, repeat”, via “Deployment creates a new pod”.
steps: One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: The database blips and every pod restarts in a loop. What is misconfigured?

choices.label: The readiness probe checks the database
The rolling update is too fast
The liveness probe checks the database

questions.explanation: Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: A node running three checkout pods dies. What does Kubernetes do?

choices.label: Schedules replacement pods on healthy nodes
Waits for the node to come back

questions.explanation: Controllers restore the declared state.

questions.prompt: Order one step of a rolling deploy.
questions.explanation: Old pods leave only after new ones are ready.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start in seconds while a VM takes minutes?

choices.label: Containers only run on bare metal
It shares the host kernel instead of booting its own OS

questions.explanation: No guest OS boot.

questions.prompt: You declared 5 replicas of checkout and one crashes. What happens?

choices.label: Nothing until you run kubectl again
Kubernetes sees 4 running instead of 5 and starts a new pod

questions.explanation: Reconciliation loops close the gap.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and start in seconds.
Failing it removes the pod from traffic without restarting it.
Failing it restarts the container.

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention
cards.body: Low contention (editing your own profile): optimistic, no waiting. High contention on one row (the last Tatkal seat): pessimistic or atomic updates, because optimistic retries would mostly fail.

cards.title: Optimistic update
cards.body: 4 steps from “Read row with version 7” to “0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry”, via “Compute new value”.
steps: 0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external payment API. The lock lives for seconds and everything else queues behind it. Keep lock scopes short.

questions.prompt: Thousands of users race for the last 10 seats on one train at 10:00. Which approach suits the seat row?

choices.label: Pessimistic locking or an atomic conditional update

questions.explanation: Under heavy contention optimistic retries mostly fail and waste work.

questions.prompt: An optimistic UPDATE ... WHERE version = 7 changes 0 rows. What happened?

choices.label: Another writer changed the row first; re-read and retry or report a conflict

questions.explanation: 0 affected rows is the conflict signal.

questions.prompt: Users edit their own address once in a while. Which approach fits?

choices.label: Pessimistic locks held for the whole session

questions.explanation: Conflicts are rare, so avoid waiting on locks.

flashcards.front: How does optimistic locking detect conflicts?
flashcards.back: A version check in the UPDATE; 0 rows updated means retry.
High contention on the same rows.

flashcards.front: What should never happen inside a lock?
flashcards.back: Slow external calls like payment APIs.

title: OT vs CRDT
objectives: Explain why collaborative editing needs conflict resolution
Know which needs a central server

cards.title: Concurrent edits collide
cards.body: Two people type into the same Google Doc paragraph at once. If each simply applies the other’s edit at the original position, their copies diverge.

cards.title: OT vs CRDT
cards.body: Operational Transformation rewrites incoming operations against concurrent ones, usually through a central server that orders them. CRDTs design data types whose merges always converge, so peers can sync in any order, even offline.

cards.title: Two users insert at once
cards.body: 4 steps from “A inserts “X” at position 5” to “Both copies converge”, via “B deletes position 2”.
steps: Server transforms A’s insert to position 4

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using last-write-wins on whole documents. One user’s entire edit disappears. Merge at the operation or character level.

questions.prompt: An app must let users edit notes offline on flights and merge later without a central server. Which fits better?

choices.label: Operational Transformation with a single ordering server

questions.explanation: CRDT merges are order-independent, which suits offline and peer-to-peer sync.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong with last-write-wins on the whole document?

choices.label: One person’s concurrent edits are silently lost

questions.explanation: Merging at operation level preserves both edits.

questions.prompt: Why does classic OT usually have a central server?

choices.label: Because OT cannot run in browsers
To give every operation a single order to transform against

questions.explanation: A single order makes transformation tractable.

flashcards.front: What does OT usually rely on?
flashcards.back: A central server that orders and transforms operations.
Replicas converge regardless of merge order, so offline sync works.
It silently discards concurrent edits.
